questions.q: Why is presenting Phase 1 to Meridian's board a different task than reading Lesson 18's ADR aloud?
options: ADRs are only written after a board presentation, never before one
The board needs a go/no-go decision framed in business terms, not the implementation record aimed at future builders and maintainers
The board already read the ADR in advance, so the presentation only needs to summarize it
The board's decision doesn't depend on any of the chapter's actual decisions
questions.explain: The ADR and the presentation share the same facts but serve different audiences and different decisions -- the board needs to decide whether to proceed, not maintain the build.

questions.q: What should a board presentation of this capstone open with?
options: The exact Script Include code from Lesson 15
A detailed walkthrough of the REST Message configuration from Lesson 16
An apology for what didn't get built in Phase 1
The business outcome -- a working Service Desk in pilot, respecting domain boundaries, inside the approved timeline -- before any individual technical decision
questions.explain: Leading with the outcome gives the board something to evaluate before any individual decision; opening with implementation detail loses a non-technical room immediately.

questions.q: How does the Prairie View integration ADR's "consequences" section translate for a board audience?
options: The board only needs to know that an integration exists, not what it costs
Prairie View's data will never be available in ServiceNow under any circumstances
Worker data can be up to fifteen minutes out of date, which is acceptable for a help desk but would not be acceptable for payroll
The integration has no real tradeoffs worth mentioning to the board
questions.explain: The reasoning stays identical to Lesson 18's ADR -- a staleness window accepted as reasonable for HR data feeding a help desk -- only the vocabulary changes for the audience.

questions.q: Why does Prairie View specifically need to hear that they pilot last, not first?
options: Because St. Catherine's and Lakeshore refused to pilot first
Because Prairie View's system has no integration at all
Because Prairie View's IT team asked to go last for no stated reason
Because Lesson 13 made their trust concern, after a prior forced consolidation went badly, a real requirement -- piloting last lets the plan absorb early defects somewhere else first
questions.explain: Lesson 13 and 18 both treat Prairie View's process concern as a real requirement, and the staged go-live plan -- piloting at the most mature site first -- is the concrete answer to it.

questions.q: Why does one combined presentation work for St. Catherine's, Lakeshore, and Prairie View representatives sitting in the same room, instead of requiring three separate ones?
options: Because none of the three systems actually has a distinct concern worth naming
Because each stakeholder's specific concern from Lesson 13 is named by name inside the same presentation, rather than folded into one generic update
Because board presentations never need to address individual stakeholder concerns
Because Lakeshore and Prairie View's concerns are identical to St. Catherine's
questions.explain: Naming each system's specific worry -- category detail, local control, sequencing and trust -- by name in one room is what makes a single presentation serve three different audiences.
